newsitem.title: USA: Florida to launch assault on Medfly.
newsitem.headline: Florida to launch assault on Medfly.

text.p: Florida will launch an aerial assault Thursday in a bid to control an infestation of the Mediterranean fruit fly, a tenacious pest that threatens the state's $6 billion agriculture industry, officials said Wednesday.
A helicopter will drop sticky bait laced with the pesticide malathion over an area of more than 70 square miles in Tampa and its suburbs, officials said at a news conference.

The Mediterranean fruit fly is considered one of the most economically damaging pests because it can tolerate cold weather and feeds on a wide variety of fruit. Florida is the nation's largest citrus producer and second-largest vegetable producer.

Since May 28, 51 flies or larvae have turned up in traps hung from fruit trees in the Tampa area. A single female or three males would have been enough to trigger an eradication program, Florida Department of Agriculture spokesman Richard Gaskalla said.
"We have both males and females, and of course the presence of larvae prove that we have a breeding population here," he said. "On the anxiety meter, I would give this a six or seven."

The Medfly is harmless to humans but can damage more than 250 varieties of fruits and vegetables, including citrus and tomatoes, Florida's largest cash crops. Local farmers have already harvested most of the tomato crop, picking the fruit early to get it out from under the spray program.

Spraying will start at dawn Thursday, with the helicopter dropping malathion-laced bait from 200 feet. By Saturday, several DC-3 mosquito treatment aircraft will join the battle and spraying will continue intermittently for 60 days, through two life cycles of the pest.
Sections of Tampa and its suburbs will be sprayed directly. All of the city and surrounding area are in a quarantine zone from which fruit may not be taken without special inspection.

Officials maintain that the malathion-laced droplets of bait pose no threat to humans or animals, or to most other insects. At the same time they ask residents to stay indoors during the spraying, to keep pets indoors and to wash cars immediately to remove the sticky mix before it damages paint.
The spray aircraft will avoid the city zoo, open bodies of water, hospitals and large new car lots.
